differential: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
This acute inflammatory polyneuropathy often presents with rapidly progressing, symmetric sensory disturbances and is a key consideration in a young person.
Multiple Sclerosis
Paresthesias are a classic initial symptom of this demyelinating CNS disease, which commonly first affects young adults.
Transverse Myelitis
Acute inflammation of the spinal cord can cause bilateral sensory symptoms below the level of the lesion, fitting the arm involvement if the cervical cord is affected.
Anxiety/Hyperventilation Syndrome
This is a common, benign cause of bilateral acral paresthesias in young people due to respiratory alkalosis.
Cervical Myelopathy
Compression of the cervical spinal cord, possibly from an acute disc herniation, can lead to bilateral sensory symptoms in the upper extremities.
eliminated: Unilateral Mononeuropathy
The patient's symptoms are bilateral, making a single nerve entrapment like carpal tunnel syndrome an incomplete explanation.
Stroke
A single cerebrovascular event is unlikely to produce isolated and symmetric paresthesias in both arms.
Diabetic Neuropathy
This is a chronic, length-dependent process that typically begins in the feet, and there is no history of diabetes.

differential: Lead poisoning
This is a classic cause of bilateral, motor-predominant radial neuropathy, presenting with wrist drop.
Radial neuropathy from compression
This is the most common cause of wrist drop, but the bilateral nature suggests an unusual compressive event or a systemic susceptibility.
Vasculitic neuropathy
A systemic vasculitis can cause mononeuritis multiplex, which could present as bilateral, asymmetric damage to the radial nerves.
Guillain-Barré syndrome
This acute polyneuropathy can present with bilateral weakness and paresthesias, and while a pure radial nerve pattern is atypical, it is possible in certain variants.
Bilateral C7 radiculopathy
Compression of the C7 nerve roots bilaterally can cause weakness in wrist extension, though the sensory pattern is less specific than a pure radial neuropathy.
eliminated: Carpal tunnel syndrome
The symptoms are in a radial nerve distribution (posterior forearm, wrist extensors), not the median nerve distribution.
Stroke
A central lesion is unlikely given the bilateral, symmetric, and peripheral nature of the findings without upper motor neuron signs.

differential: Radial Nerve Compression Neuropathy
The clinical signs of wrist drop and sensory loss, combined with EMG/NCS findings localizing a conduction block at the elbow, are classic for compression at the spiral groove.
Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP)
This genetic condition explains a predisposition to developing bilateral compression neuropathies, especially in a young patient.
Lead Poisoning
This toxic exposure is a classic, though uncommon, cause of a predominantly motor neuropathy affecting the radial nerves bilaterally.
Vasculitic Mononeuritis Multiplex
Systemic vasculitis can cause ischemic injury to multiple individual nerves, presenting as an acute, asymmetric pattern such as bilateral radial palsies.
Bilateral Posterior Interosseous Nerve Syndrome
This diagnosis considers a more distal compression of the radial nerve's motor branch, though it less commonly explains the sensory deficits noted.
eliminated: Cervical Radiculopathy
Nerve conduction studies localized the pathology to the radial nerve at the elbow, effectively ruling out a primary problem at the nerve root level.
Brachial Plexopathy
Electrodiagnostic findings point to a lesion at the elbow, which is distal to the brachial plexus.
Guillain-Barré Syndrome
The presentation is focal to the radial nerves rather than the typical ascending and symmetric pattern of GBS.

differential: Tourniquet-induced radial neuropathy
The patient's most severe symptoms are on the left side, corresponding directly with the location and timing of prolonged tourniquet use during recent surgery.
Positioning-related radial neuropathy
Milder symptoms in the contralateral arm can be explained by prolonged pressure on that arm due to positioning during the lengthy surgical procedure.
Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP)
An underlying genetic susceptibility could explain the development of significant bilateral compression neuropathies from the surgical procedure.
Vasculitic neuropathy (Mononeuritis Multiplex)
This systemic inflammatory condition can present with multiple, asymmetric peripheral nerve palsies and can be triggered by the stress of surgery.
Lead Poisoning
This is a classic, albeit rare, systemic cause of bilateral radial neuropathy (wrist drop), though the acute onset and asymmetry make it less likely.
eliminated: Cervical Radiculopathy
EMG and NCS findings localize the lesion to the peripheral radial nerve at the elbow, which is inconsistent with a nerve root impingement in the neck.
Brachial Plexitis (Parsonage-Turner Syndrome)
The findings are focal to the radial nerve distribution, whereas brachial plexitis typically involves multiple nerves of the brachial plexus.
Stroke
The symptoms and electrodiagnostic findings are characteristic of a peripheral nerve injury, not a central nervous system lesion like a stroke.

differential: Multiple Sclerosis
This demyelinating CNS disease commonly affects young adults and can cause a cervical myelopathy presenting with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.
Transverse Myelitis
This diagnosis represents inflammation of the spinal cord, which directly explains the combination of sensory deficits, weakness, and upper motor neuron signs.
Syringomyelia
A fluid-filled cavity within the cervical spinal cord could cause a central cord syndrome, explaining the specific motor and sensory deficits along with the upper motor neuron findings.
Spinal Cord Tumor
An intramedullary neoplasm can compress neural tracts and gray matter, producing the observed combination of focal weakness and widespread upper motor neuron signs.
Vitamin B12 Deficiency
This deficiency can cause subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, leading to both upper motor neuron signs and a peripheral neuropathy that could mimic this presentation.
eliminated: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
The presence of hyperreflexia and Babinski signs are definitive upper motor neuron findings, which rules out this lower motor neuron disease.
Peripheral Nerve Entrapment (e.g., Radial Neuropathy)
This diagnosis is excluded by the bilateral symptoms and the presence of upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski sign), which indicate a central nervous system origin.

differential: Multiple Sclerosis
This demyelinating CNS disease is common in young adults and can cause UMN signs, with the peripheral findings potentially representing a concurrent pressure palsy.
Cervical Myelopathy
A single lesion in the cervical spinal cord could compress both the corticospinal tracts to cause UMN signs and the nerve roots or anterior horn cells to cause LMN signs.
Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
This diagnosis classically presents with a combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs, which are both clearly present in this patient.
Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP)
This genetic condition perfectly explains the bilateral radial nerve palsies at a common entrapment site, though it would not account for the UMN signs.
Lead Toxicity
This intoxication can cause a motor-predominant peripheral neuropathy, classically affecting the radial nerve, as well as central nervous system dysfunction.
eliminated: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
This diagnosis is inconsistent with the patient's upper motor neuron signs of hyperreflexia and upgoing Babinski signs.
Radial Nerve Entrapment
As a sole diagnosis, this is ruled out because it does not explain the bilateral symptoms or the upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs.
C7 Radiculopathy
This diagnosis alone does not account for the upper motor neuron signs in the lower extremities or the EMG/NCS findings localizing the neuropathy to the elbow.

differential: Tourniquet-induced radial nerve palsy
The recent history of prolonged tourniquet use on the left arm directly explains the acute onset of left-sided radial nerve deficits confirmed by EMG/NCS.
Multiple sclerosis
The presence of hyperreflexia and bilateral Babinski signs in a young adult strongly suggests a co-existing central nervous system demyelinating process.
Radial nerve compression neuropathy (Saturday night palsy)
This is a common cause of radial nerve palsy and could explain the bilateral symptoms due to positioning during or after surgery.
Cervical radiculopathy
This diagnosis is considered for upper extremity neurological deficits, although it is less likely given EMG/NCS findings that localize the pathology distally to the radial nerve.
Lead poisoning (Plumbism)
This classic cause of bilateral motor-predominant radial neuropathy is a consideration given the bilateral findings, though it is rare and less likely than an iatrogenic cause.
eliminated: Guillain-Barré syndrome
This patient presents with hyperreflexia and focal weakness, which is contrary to the typical ascending symmetric paralysis with areflexia seen in GBS.
Brachial plexopathy
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies localized the lesion to the radial nerve at the elbow, making a more proximal injury at the brachial plexus unlikely.
Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
The patient's young age, acute onset, and significant sensory deficits are not characteristic of ALS.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The presence of hyperreflexia and upgoing Babinski sign argues against radial nerve injury, which would not cause upper motor neuron signs.
